    Our project so far

    What we are building.

    One compact flat base. A front panel holds the screen and the start button. Behind it, four servo grippers sit on a plate and hold the cube from four sides, with all the wiring tucked underneath.

    How it automates

    It senses, decides and acts without a person pushing buttons.

    A person places the cube and presses start. Everything else, from deciding the moves to turning the faces, happens on its own.

    Input

    Start button and camera

    A start button begins each run. One camera under the cube reads all 54 stickers.

    Decision

    The controller

    Code checks the colors make a legal cube, then finds the short list of moves that solves it.

    Output

    Servo grippers

    The Arduino Uno drives eight servos in four grippers, which turn the faces one move at a time. A front screen shows what it is doing.

      Problem& Research

      Who the robot is for, the experience it creates, and the projects we studied first.

        The experience we are designing

        Hand over a scrambled cube. Watch it get solved.

        Solving a cube by hand takes real skill. We want a machine that does it in front of you, with no one pressing buttons in between.

        Who it is for

        Curious students and puzzle fans

        Anyone who has a cube they cannot solve and wants to see how a machine reads and solves it. Draft wording for the team to refine.

        The gap

        Scanning is the slow part

        In the open-source robot we studied, a person taps to scan each of the six faces on a phone. We want one placement to read the whole cube.

        Existing projects

        What we studied.

        Three builds we studied.

        Study 1

        Rubik's cube solving robot (video)

        A video of a cube-solving robot that the team is studying for how it grips and turns the cube.

        Video

        Study 2

        Arduino Rubik robot solver with 8 servo motors

        By Emanuel Marques, Sep 2021. An Arduino Uno with a 16-channel servo board and 8 servos. An Android app captures the cube colors and sends them over a Bluetooth module. It solves with the CFOP method.

        Video

        Study 3

        CubeStormer 3, the record-breaking LEGO robot

        By David Gilday and Mike Dobson, 2014. A LEGO Mindstorms robot with four robotic hands and a Samsung Galaxy S4 phone. It solved a cube in 3.253 seconds at the Big Bang Fair in Birmingham, England, a world record. It shows how fast a four-sided gripper design can be.

        Wikipedia

        Page 04 of 10

        Brainstorm& Ideas

        The three ideas we compared, how we picked one, and how the design changed from the first sketch to now.

          Three ideas

          What we could have built.

          Each idea needed a sensor, an action, and a build that fits in 2 ft × 2 ft.

          Idea 1

          Rubik's cube solving robot

          Four servo grippers hold a cube and turn its faces. A camera reads all 54 stickers, the Arduino works out the moves, and a screen shows progress.

          Sensor: camera and start button. Action: eight servos.

          Idea 2

          UNO card dealer

          A turning dealer with an ultrasonic sensor that sweeps 360 degrees to find each player, then deals one card to each.

          Sensor: ultrasonic. Action: a servo that turns and a motor that pushes a card out.

          Idea 3

          Mini golf

          A table-top mini golf hole with a sensor that detects the ball and a motor that moves an obstacle or keeps score.

          Sensor: ball detector. Action: a motor and a score display.

          Decision matrix

          Why the cube solver won.

          We scored each idea from 1 to 5 on what the project needs. Bigger weights count more.

          Criterion (score 1 to 5)WeightCube solverCard dealerMini golf
          Has a sensor and an action5543
          Fits in 2 ft × 2 ft4454
          Stands out and goes above and beyond5532
          Can be finished by the end of the semester4344
          Parts we have or can get free3443
          The whole team is comfortable with it3443
          Weighted total (out of 120)1029575

          The cube solver scores 102 of 120, ahead of the card dealer (95) and mini golf (75). It stands out the most and it needs both a sensor and a real mechanism. The team agreed on it and the teacher approved it on Oct 22.

          How the design changed

          From first sketch to final base.

          Each stage fixed a problem we found in the one before.

          Stage 1 · Oct 21 to 22

          Pick the idea and the first model

          We shortlisted three ideas and the cube solver won. Mr. Savino approved it on Oct 22. Our very first 3D draft used simple shapes: four grippers around the cube, a front screen on a stand, wires inside and a base of 17.5 × 20 in.

          Stage 2 · Oct 22

          A slanted control panel

          The next draft added a slanted front panel for the screen and start button, and the base grew to 17.5 × 23 in. The shapes were still simple placeholders for the real parts.

          Stage 3 · Oct 23 to 29

          One arm first

          Shremat modeled a single gripper and motor assembly, and Yatish modeled the grabber. All four arms are the same part, so one design is printed four times.

          Stage 4 · Oct 29 to 30

          Four grippers on one plate

          The arm was placed four times around the cube on a single flat plate. This CAD picture is the first full gripper station.

          Stage 5 · Oct 30 to Nov 2

          A compact base, then too big to print

          The screen and button holder hid the wires inside. We made the base as small as possible with the screen at the front and the mechanism at the back, then found it was too big to print in one piece.

          Stage 6 · Nov 3 to 5

          The screen moves onto a Raspberry Pi

          The colour screen now plugs straight onto a Raspberry Pi that sits in a printed pocket in the front. The Arduino stays the boss and talks to the Pi over USB.

          Stage 7 · Nov 6

          Four tiles, keys and a flat plate

          The base became four white tiles, each printed with its own holders and fitted one at a time, then locked from underneath with four black butterfly keys. The mechanism plate is now flat (257 × 240 mm) with holes for the camera, cables and screws, and the cables run through it.

              Wiring& Circuit

              How power and signals move through the build, and the safety rules we follow while wiring it.

                Interactive

                The wiring in 3D.

                Only the electronics, no base and no grippers: the breadboard, Arduino, Raspberry Pi, power banks and every wire, hole by hole in 14 steps. The whole robot is on the Design page.

                Wiring guideFull screen
                System overview

                Signals and power.

                Each servo has one cable with three wires (signal, power, ground) that plugs into a breadboard. Servos get their own power bank so they never pull power from the Arduino's 5V pin. The whole robot runs from batteries, with no wall outlet.

                Picture guide

                See what plugs in where.

                Three pictures: the Arduino pins we use, one servo cable, and the breadboard. The same colors are used in the 3D model and the diagram above.

                Arduino Uno

                The pins we use

                ■ D2 to D9 servo signals · ■ D11 start button · ■ D12, D13 camera · USB socket: status messages to the Raspberry Pi · ■ 5V · GND

                One servo

                Three wires, one plug

                Brown goes on the − pin. If a plug goes on backwards, the servo will not move and can get damaged.

                Breadboard

                Eight plugs for eight servos

                The 3D model shows these wires in place. Open the 3D model on the Design page and set the top sheet to Clear.

                Wire it in this order

                Eleven steps, with everything unplugged.

                1. Unplug both USB cables and the power banksNothing is powered while you wire.
                2. Put the capacitor across the breadboard railsLong leg to the + rail, short leg (the stripe) to the − rail.
                3. Join the groundsThe breadboard − rail goes to an Arduino GND pin. The servo power bank's black wire goes to that rail.
                4. Run the eight signal wiresServo plug 1 signal column to D2, 2 to D3, up to 8 to D9. Label both ends.
                5. Set the plate on the rails, screws outThe plate with the four arms rests on the two side rails. Keep every servo cable loose beside it.
                6. Route each top (turn) servo cableStart at the back of the servo. Lead the cable down the back edge of the tall post, lay it flat along the plate, and push the plug down through the hole on the far side of the arm. Pull the slack through underneath.
                7. Route each slide servo cableStart at the top back of the slide servo. Let it fall down the outside, lay it flat past the gear, and push the plug down through the hole beside the gear. Keep it clear of the gear teeth.
                8. Repeat for all four arms, then screw the plate downRight, left, front and back, 8 cables in all. Leave a small loop on each so the arm can slide 30.5 mm.
                9. Plug in the servo cables one at a timeBrown on −, red on +, orange on S. Use extension cables where the cable is too short.
                10. Wire the start button and the Raspberry PiButton: one side to D11, the other to GND. Screen: eight wires from the colour screen to the Pi header (GND pin 6, VCC pin 1, LED pin 17, SCK pin 23, MOSI pin 19, CS pin 24, DC pin 22, RESET pin 18). USB: logic power bank to the Pi's micro-USB socket, and a USB cable from the Pi to the Arduino.
                11. Check twice, then power upPlug in the logic power bank's USB cable to the Pi first (it powers the Arduino through the second USB cable), then connect the servo power bank's wires to the rails. Ask a teammate or the teacher to check the wiring before the first power-up.
                Pin list

                Every pin we use.

                SignalComponentArduino pin
                Right turn servo signalServoD2
                Right slide servo signalServoD3
                Left turn servo signalServoD4
                Left slide servo signalServoD5
                Front turn servo signalServoD6
                Front slide servo signalServoD7
                Back turn servo signalServoD8
                Back slide servo signalServoD9
                Start buttonPush button to GNDD11

                Camera linkESP32-CAM, through a 2-resistor divider on the Arduino's sending lineD12 (RX), D13 (TX)
                Safety

                While we wire.

                • Unplug the Arduino before changing any wiring.
                • Low voltage only: USB or approved battery packs. No wall-outlet wiring, ever.
                • Servos get their own power bank, not the Arduino's 5V pin.
                Page 08 of 10

                Code

                The program's logic in plain steps, then in pseudocode. The full commented Arduino code goes here as we write it.

                  Flowchart

                  One full run.

                  1. Wait for the start buttonA person places the cube and presses start. A cube-in-place sensor checks it is there.
                  2. Show "Working" on the screenThe status screen follows every step.
                  3. Test mode: load the stored move listA short saved list of moves is used to test the grippers.
                  4. Scan the cube firstThe camera board sends the 54 colors. Not a legal cube: show "Scan again" and go back.
                  5. Find the solutionThe camera board or a phone finds the moves and sends the list to the Arduino.
                  6. Do each moveThe right servo turns the face, the grippers slide out of the way when needed, and the Arduino waits until it is done.
                  7. Show "Done" and the move countThe output is a finished cube. Then go back to waiting for the start button.
                  Pseudocode

                  The same logic, as code.

                  // Draft. The full commented Arduino code replaces this later.
loop forever:
  wait until start_button is pressed and cube_is_in_place
  show("Working")
  moves = stored_undo_moves                     // test moves
  // normal run: moves = scan_and_solve()  (camera board sends the move list)
  for each move in moves:
      turn_face(move)                           // slide servos retract, turn servo spins 90 degrees
      show_progress(move_number, total_moves)
  show("Done", move_count)
                  Full code

                  Commented Arduino sketch.

                  The Arduino sketch Shremat began writing on Day 10. It reads the start button, asks the camera board for a solution and falls back to a stored test list of moves, turns each face with the grippers, and shows progress and the move count on the screen. Servo angles and delays are starting values that are tuned on the real robot.

                  // ============================================================
// Cube Solver - Team Double Stuffed Oreo
// Arduino Uno. Four grippers, each with a SLIDE servo (in/out)
// and a TURN servo (spins the face). Start button, status messages over USB to a Raspberry Pi (colour screen),
// camera board on a serial link.
//
// Test list: a known scramble stored in the sketch, used to test the grippers.
// Normal run: the camera board sends the solution as text,
//            for example  "F R' B2 L"  ending with a newline.
//
// Gripper numbers: 0 = Front, 1 = Right, 2 = Back, 3 = Left.
// Move letters:    F R B L  (U and D need the cube flipped,
//                  see the note in doMove).
// A letter alone = clockwise, ' = counterclockwise, 2 = half turn.
// ============================================================

#include <Servo.h>
#include <SoftwareSerial.h>

// ---------- Pins (match the wiring page) ----------
const int TURN_PINS[4]  = {2, 4, 6, 8};   // spins each gripper (D2 = Arm 1 turn, D4 = Arm 2 turn, ...)
const int SLIDE_PINS[4] = {3, 5, 7, 9};   // slides each gripper in and out (D3 = Arm 1 slide, ...)
const int START_BUTTON  = 11;             // start button to GND (INPUT_PULLUP)
const int CAM_RX        = 12;             // from camera board (through 1k/2k divider)
const int CAM_TX        = 13;             // to camera board

// ---------- Servo angles (tune these on the real robot) ----------
const int SLIDE_IN  = 40;     // gripper holding the cube
const int SLIDE_OUT = 140;    // gripper pulled back
const int TURN_0    = 0;      // turn servo at rest
const int TURN_90   = 90;
const int TURN_180  = 180;

// ---------- Timing (milliseconds) ----------
const int GRIP_TIME    = 350;   // wait for a gripper to slide in or out
const int TURN_TIME    = 500;   // wait for a turn servo to finish
const int DEBOUNCE_MS  = 40;

// ---------- Objects ----------
Servo turnServo[4];
Servo slideServo[4];
SoftwareSerial cam(CAM_RX, CAM_TX);

// ---------- Test list: stored moves (the undo list for a known scramble) ----------
// Each move is a letter and a count: 1 = clockwise, 3 = counterclockwise, 2 = half turn.
struct Move { char face; byte turns; };
const Move STORED[] = { {'F',1}, {'R',3}, {'B',2}, {'L',1}, {'F',3} };   // placeholder
const int STORED_COUNT = sizeof(STORED) / sizeof(STORED[0]);

// ---------- Move list used in the current run ----------
const int MAX_MOVES = 60;
Move queue[MAX_MOVES];
int queueLen = 0;

// ============================================================
// Screen
// ============================================================
void showScreen(const char* line1, const char* line2) {
  // The Raspberry Pi reads this line from the USB cable and draws it
  // in colour on the screen:  "text one|text two"
  Serial.print(line1);
  Serial.print('|');
  Serial.println(line2);
}

void showProgress(int done, int total) {
  char buf[16];
  snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "%d / %d", done, total);
  showScreen("Working", buf);
}

// ============================================================
// Moving the robot
// ============================================================
int gripperFor(char face) {
  switch (face) {
    case 'F': return 0;
    case 'R': return 1;
    case 'B': return 2;
    case 'L': return 3;
  }
  return -1;   // U or D: not handled by a gripper directly
}

// Turn one face. turns: 1 = clockwise, 3 = counterclockwise, 2 = half turn.
void turnFace(int g, byte turns) {
  // 1. Put the turn servo at the right starting angle while the gripper is pulled back
  int startAngle = (turns == 3) ? TURN_90 : TURN_0;
  int endAngle   = (turns == 3) ? TURN_0  : (turns == 2 ? TURN_180 : TURN_90);
  turnServo[g].write(startAngle);
  delay(TURN_TIME);

  // 2. Grip the cube
  slideServo[g].write(SLIDE_IN);
  delay(GRIP_TIME);

  // 3. Spin the face
  turnServo[g].write(endAngle);
  delay(TURN_TIME);

  // 4. Let go and return to rest
  slideServo[g].write(SLIDE_OUT);
  delay(GRIP_TIME);
  turnServo[g].write(TURN_0);
  delay(TURN_TIME);
}

// Run one move. Returns false if the move cannot be done by the grippers.
bool doMove(const Move& m) {
  int g = gripperFor(m.face);
  if (g < 0) {
    // U and D: the cube would have to be flipped first so that the face is on a side.
    // Not built yet. The solver/camera side should only send F R B L moves for now.
    return false;
  }
  turnFace(g, m.turns);
  return true;
}

void releaseAll() {
  for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    slideServo[i].write(SLIDE_OUT);
    turnServo[i].write(TURN_0);
  }
  delay(GRIP_TIME + TURN_TIME);
}

// ============================================================
// Reading moves
// ============================================================
void loadStoredMoves() {
  queueLen = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < STORED_COUNT && queueLen < MAX_MOVES; i++) {
    queue[queueLen++] = STORED[i];
  }
}

// Turn text such as "F R' B2 L" into the queue. Returns the number of moves.
int parseMoves(const char* text) {
  queueLen = 0;
  int i = 0;
  while (text[i] != '\0' && queueLen < MAX_MOVES) {
    char c = text[i];
    if (c == 'F' || c == 'R' || c == 'B' || c == 'L' || c == 'U' || c == 'D') {
      byte turns = 1;
      if (text[i + 1] == '\'') { turns = 3; i++; }
      else if (text[i + 1] == '2') { turns = 2; i++; }
      queue[queueLen].face = c;
      queue[queueLen].turns = turns;
      queueLen++;
    }
    i++;
  }
  return queueLen;
}

// Ask the camera board to scan and solve, then read the move list.
// Returns true if a list came back in time.
bool askCameraForSolution(unsigned long timeoutMs) {
  while (cam.available()) cam.read();     // clear old bytes
  cam.println("SOLVE");
  char line[200];
  int n = 0;
  unsigned long start = millis();
  while (millis() - start < timeoutMs) {
    if (cam.available()) {
      char c = cam.read();
      if (c == '\n') {
        line[n] = '\0';
        return parseMoves(line) > 0;
      }
      if (n < (int)sizeof(line) - 1) line[n++] = c;
    }
  }
  return false;
}

// ============================================================
// Button
// ============================================================
bool startPressed() {
  if (digitalRead(START_BUTTON) == LOW) {
    delay(DEBOUNCE_MS);
    if (digitalRead(START_BUTTON) == LOW) {
      while (digitalRead(START_BUTTON) == LOW) { }   // wait for release
      return true;
    }
  }
  return false;
}

// ============================================================
// Main program
// ============================================================
void setup() {
  for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    turnServo[i].attach(TURN_PINS[i]);
    slideServo[i].attach(SLIDE_PINS[i]);
  }
  releaseAll();

  pinMode(START_BUTTON, INPUT_PULLUP);
  cam.begin(9600);
  Serial.begin(115200);             // USB cable to the Raspberry Pi
  showScreen("Ready", "Press start");
}

void loop() {
  if (!startPressed()) return;

  // Camera first: if the camera board answers, use its solution.
  // If not, fall back to the stored test moves.
  showScreen("Scanning", "");
  if (!askCameraForSolution(8000)) {
    loadStoredMoves();
  }

  showProgress(0, queueLen);
  int skipped = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < queueLen; i++) {
    if (!doMove(queue[i])) skipped++;
    showProgress(i + 1, queueLen);
  }

  char buf[16];
  snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "%d moves", queueLen - skipped);
  showScreen("Done", buf);
  if (skipped > 0) {
    delay(1500);
    snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "%d skipped", skipped);
    showScreen("Check U/D", buf);
  }
}
                  Screen program

                  The Raspberry Pi side.

                  The Arduino prints a line like Working|12 / 30 on the USB cable. This small Python program on the Raspberry Pi reads each line and draws it in colour on the 2.8 in screen. It is a starting point that we have not run on the real board yet, so expect to adjust the port name, the screen rotation and the colours.

                  # Setup on the Pi (one time):
#   sudo raspi-config  ->  Interface Options  ->  SPI  ->  Enable
#   sudo pip3 install adafruit-circuitpython-rgb-display pyserial pillow
# Save as screen.py and run:  python3 screen.py
import time
import serial
import board
import digitalio
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont
from adafruit_rgb_display import ili9341

PORT = "/dev/ttyACM0"          # the Arduino (clones may show up as /dev/ttyUSB0)

# Screen wiring (see the wiring page): CS = pin 24 (CE0), DC = pin 22 (GPIO25), RESET = pin 18 (GPIO24)
cs  = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.CE0)
dc  = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.D25)
rst = digitalio.DigitalInOut(board.D24)
disp = ili9341.ILI9341(board.SPI(), cs=cs, dc=dc, rst=rst,
                       baudrate=24000000, rotation=90)   # landscape; try 270 if it is upside down
W, H = disp.width, disp.height

big   = ImageFont.truetype("/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf", 44)
small = ImageFont.truetype("/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans.ttf", 30)

COLORS = {"Ready": (60, 220, 130), "Working": (255, 210, 60), "Scanning": (80, 200, 255),
          "Done": (60, 220, 130), "Check U/D": (255, 90, 90)}

def show(line1, line2):
    img = Image.new("RGB", (W, H), (5, 18, 42))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
    d.rectangle((0, 0, W, 50), fill=(23, 178, 106))
    d.text((12, 4), "CUBE ROBOT", font=small, fill=(255, 255, 255))
    d.text((12, 80), line1, font=big, fill=COLORS.get(line1, (255, 255, 255)))
    d.text((12, 150), line2, font=small, fill=(143, 208, 255))
    disp.image(img)

show("Starting", "")
while True:
    try:
        with serial.Serial(PORT, 115200, timeout=1) as arduino:   # opening the port resets the Arduino, which is fine at start-up
            while True:
                line = arduino.readline().decode("utf-8", "ignore").strip()
                if "|" in line:
                    a, b = line.split("|", 1)
                    show(a, b)
    except serial.SerialException:
        show("No Arduino", "check the USB cable")
        time.sleep(2)

                  To start it automatically, add python3 /home/pi/screen.py & to /etc/rc.local above the line exit 0. The Raspberry Pi Model B takes about a minute to start, so the screen shows the start message a little after the Arduino is ready.

                    Day 14 · Mon Nov 9 · Team (all four present)

                    Today's goal

                    Update the design so the robot can also be controlled from a phone, learn to print our own parts, and get Nazar and Hlib working on the website.

                    What we did

                    We switched the regular Arduino for a WiFi-based one, so we can control the robot from a phone as well. Yatish and Shremat learned how to upload an STL file to the Bambu printer, add supports and start a print, so we can print our parts ourselves and do not need Coach Savino to print them for us. In the meantime Nazar and Hlib began working on the website for this project and on their own websites, so they get familiar with it before their capstone project and are not starting from nothing.

                    Problems and solutions

                    A regular Arduino has no WiFi, so it could not take commands from a phone. Switching to a WiFi-based board fixes that. Printing used to depend on Coach Savino, and now two of us can run the Bambu printer on our own.
